title: Rethinking Joint Maximum Mean Discrepancy for Visual Domain Adaptation

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 1 reports OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC average as 90.1, but summing the six listed per-task values (96.1, 95.3, 77.6, 98.1, 77.1, 99.1) gives 543.3/6 ≈ 90.6. The text then says 'OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC achieves the best average results among all compared approaches, with 0.3% and 0.5% improvements over ... RSDA-MSTN'. On Office-31, RSDA-MSTN is 91.2, and OGL2P+JMMD-HSIC is neither best nor better than RSDA-MSTN.

Table 6 reports OGL2P+Our average as 94.3 ± 0.7, but the listed per-task means sum to 1134.5/12 ≈ 94.5. Appendix F also claims OGL2P+Our improves over OGL2P on average by 0.4%, but the OGL2P baseline mean is 94.6, so OGL2P+Our is lower, not higher.

The text states: 'For a fair comparison, all hyper-parameters remain consistent with the three approaches. Regarding δ, we set it to 0.5 for JDA+JMMD-HSIC, and performed targeted manual tuning per dataset for the other two variants to maximize performance, with selective reporting of best results.' This is self-contradictory and explicitly admits hyperparameter cherry-picking and selective reporting, invalidating the claimed fair comparison.

The experimental setup admits that 'some baseline methods employ alternative pretrained features or fine-tuning strategies, potentially affecting direct comparability' and that 'uniformity across comparison baselines is not guaranteed.' This means the reported comparisons against baselines are not conducted under controlled, matching conditions.

The paper describes 'D²: ImageCLEF-DA, a constructed dataset synthesized for this study'. ImageCLEF-DA is a standard public domain-adaptation benchmark with Caltech-256, ImageNet ILSVRC 2012, and Pascal VOC 2012 domains; it was not synthesized for this paper.

The Representer theorem is misquoted: 'any function can be decomposed into finite values of a kernel function with corresponding coefficients.' The actual theorem says that the minimizer of a regularized empirical risk over an RKHS lies in the span of kernel evaluations at the training points. Arbitrary functions or projection matrices T are not guaranteed to have such a finite representation, so the justification for Eq. (2) is mathematically unsound as stated.

The matrix M^H is used in the 'concise HSIC' formulas but is never defined. Moreover, standard HSIC is a centered statistic, typically written as tr(K_X H K_Y H); the paper does not derive why HSIC should equal tr(K^{XX}(K^{YY}⊙M^H)) for the unspecified M^H. Without defining M^H, the HSIC term and the JMMD-HSIC objective are underspecified.

The graph-embedding identity in Eq. (6) is missing a factor of 2: for symmetric W, Σ_{i,j} w_{ij}||z_i − z_j||² = 2 tr(Z L Z^T), not tr(Z L Z^T). Consequently, Eq. (8), which rewrites the projected JMMD/HSIC traces as such sums, is also off by a factor of 2.

The Introduction states that 'the exact elimination of the tensor product remains an open problem, and derivative calculations require further careful analysis beyond the scope of this work.' Section 3.1 and Eq. (2), however, claim that the tensor-product operator disappears and that the partial derivative with respect to B is readily available. These statements directly contradict each other.

The paper repeatedly says HSIC should be maximized to increase feature-label dependence and improve discrimination, but the proposed loss in Eq. (9) adds the HSIC term with positive coefficient δ and is minimized. With the designed K⁴ this becomes a graph-Laplacian intra-class compactness regularizer; the sign/meaning of 'HSIC' relative to the stated maximization objective is inconsistent and needs clarification.
